subtitle: Bring your team’s unwritten expectations into the open, examine what they actually accomplish and agree together on a more usable way to work.
scope: For staff and team leads across DHS. This practice lab uses practice DSD work to distinguish informal expectations from verified requirements and develop an authorized team improvement. It does not establish a policy violation, revise a service rule, delegate approval authority or replace an actual reporting or accommodation process. The consultant leads the program and offers guidance and feedback; staff carry out their own work. Learning is voluntary. Keep actual protected information in its appropriate process. Excluded Native American or Tribal-specific matters go to the appropriate office within ADSA (Aging and Disability Services Administration).
introTranscript: Every team has expectations that are easier to learn by watching than by reading. A draft may be called ready only after a quiet preview; a question may be welcomed from one colleague but treated as a problem from another. Some habits make coordination easier. Others hide a decision, narrow participation or make success depend on knowing the right person. In this lab you will map a recurring expectation, examine its learned meanings, test its purpose and propose a clear work agreement within actual authority. The practice includes private reflection on your own assumptions as well as a concrete team task. You do not need to label anyone’s culture or disclose a personal history. The aim is a more understandable way of working, with real requirements preserved and hidden burdens open to examination.

lessons.title: Notice the expectation before naming a rule
lessons.summary: Separate an observed exchange, a recurring expectation and a verified requirement.
lessons.objective: Describe a team in this example exchange without assigning motive or cultural identity.
objectives: Describe a team in this example exchange without assigning motive or cultural identity.
Distinguish an observation, an inferred informal expectation and a verified requirement.
Write a specific question that can test whether an unwritten expectation recurs.
takeaways: One exchange can raise a useful question without establishing a universal rule.
An informal expectation becomes easier to examine when its words, context and consequences are visible.
Verify the actual requirement instead of treating a confident colleague’s statement as policy.
lessons.statement: Begin with what happened, then ask what people expect and why.

image.caption: A team reviews how a draft moves from preparation to a responsible decision.

intro.heading: What does ready mean here?
intro.body:
In a practice DSD planning team, a work note describes a draft as ready for review. Rowan brings it to the scheduled meeting. An experienced colleague says it should first have been previewed privately by a senior analyst. Rowan cannot find that step in the instruction. The draft may need useful preparation, but the exchange does not yet establish a formal requirement or explain who decides that it is ready. The team has a concrete question to examine.

Describe the exchange before drawing a wider conclusion. The note said ready, Rowan brought the draft, and a colleague asked for a prior preview. These are observations in the case. “People must always obtain a senior analyst’s private endorsement” is an inferred expectation. “DHS policy requires this exact preview” is a requirement claim that needs a verified source and scope. Mixing the three can turn a learning question into an unsupported accusation or a false rule.

An unwritten expectation is not necessarily a secret conspiracy. It may have developed because an earlier preview caught important mistakes, because a long-serving colleague knows a complex task, or because people learned that unprepared drafts take meeting time. It may also continue after its original purpose has changed. Ask what the expectation is supposed to accomplish and how people learn it. The answer can reveal a useful practice, a hidden burden or both.

Look for a consequence rather than only a phrase. Does a draft bypassing the preview get returned even when it meets the written criteria? Does the person receive a different explanation depending on who is present? Does the senior analyst’s availability determine whether the draft reaches the meeting? A specific consequence helps identify what makes the expectation influential. It still does not establish motive or a policy violation. Use appropriately protected work facts, not private accounts copied into a general practice worksheet.

Make the proposed pattern testable. Instead of writing “this team excludes new staff,” ask whether the preparation instructions identify the preview, its purpose, who can provide it and what happens when that person is unavailable. Compare relevant examples that use the same task and period. A draft with missing evidence is not equivalent to a complete draft that lacked an informal endorsement. Context matters to understanding which part of the work is actually producing the response.

Avoid turning individual comments into a team census. One experienced colleague may describe a personal preference, a task-specific caution or a delegated responsibility. Other colleagues may use a different path. A useful first map leaves these possibilities visible. It can mark the preview expectation as a question to confirm rather than a settled fact. That is more accurate than treating every confident statement as policy or every unexplained habit as harmful.

There is also a private reflection available here. You might remember situations in which you learned to treat senior approval as safety, or learned to regard an independent draft as competence. Those meanings can influence how you hear the exchange. You can examine your own history without making Rowan or the colleague disclose theirs. Personal insight does not become an assessed cultural position, personnel label or substitute for checking the actual work instruction.

The next step in the practice case is a bounded inquiry: clarify what ready means for this draft, whether a preview is required or optional, and which role can confirm that. Write the observation and question separately. This prepares the team to examine a real expectation without deciding the answer in advance or inventing an approval rule.

lessons.keyStatement: A useful map shows the observed event, the expectation to examine and the requirement still needing verification.

flashcards.back: An account of what was said or done in a relevant context, without an unsupported motive or group explanation.
A belief about how work should happen that may be learned through experience rather than a clear instruction. Its actual reach and effect need examination.
An applicable rule or authorized responsibility supported by its actual source and scope, not merely a confident statement.
What follows when someone meets or misses an expectation, such as a draft return, delay or response. It helps explain how the expectation operates.
A specific uncertainty that can be examined, such as whether a preview is required and how staff can obtain it. It is not a verdict about the team.

items.title: Name the task and event
items.body: Rowan submitted a draft under an instruction calling it ready. The colleague requested a prior preview. Describe the relevant task and timing so the person responsible can distinguish a missing work requirement from a preference about preparation. “The team is hostile” supplies a judgment before identifying the actual mechanism; a precise account makes that mechanism examinable.

items.title: Describe what still needs confirmation
items.body: The preview may be optional help, a documented responsibility or an informal condition that now controls access to the review. Ask which it is and how the answer can be verified. Recording uncertainty is useful: it prevents an early learning note from becoming a false policy claim or an accusation that outruns the available facts.

items.title: Look for a comparable consequence
items.body: If complete drafts without a preview are returned, identify that specific pattern and the relevant context. Compare it with drafts that actually lack necessary evidence rather than treating every return as equivalent. A difference may justify more inquiry without proving bias or motive. The map should help locate the expectation, not rank colleagues by a guessed explanation.

tabs.label: What happened
tabs.body: “The colleague asked Rowan to obtain a preview before the meeting” describes this exchange. It can be checked against the relevant work account. The statement does not establish that everyone follows the same path or that Rowan was treated differently because of identity. Keep the observed words and context useful, then identify the wider question separately. A precise observation is stronger than a dramatic conclusion because another person can examine what it actually supports.

tabs.label: What may be expected
tabs.body: “A private preview may be treated as the sign that a draft is ready” proposes an informal expectation. Test it by clarifying instructions, asking about the purpose and examining comparable work paths. If the preview is optional help, the response should not silently turn it into approval. If it is a genuine responsibility, its route needs to be clear. The expectation is a hypothesis about practice, not permission to disregard the task.

tabs.label: What is actually required
tabs.body: “This review requires a designated role’s sign-off” needs the applicable instruction and actual authority. Verify who signs, what they review and how the step is recorded. A senior colleague’s expertise can support preparation without automatically creating an approval power. Confusing expertise with authority may delay good work or bypass a real decision. The verified requirement should inform the map; the map cannot manufacture it.

check.question: A colleague says a private preview is always required, but Rowan cannot find it in the draft instruction. What is the sound next step?
check.correct: Describe the exchange and verify the preview’s purpose, scope and actual requirement before treating it as a team rule or policy.
wrong: Declare a policy violation from this exchange alone.
Treat the colleague’s confidence as proof of formal authority.
Ignore every preparation step because it is not yet understood.
check.feedbackCorrect: This preserves the observation, tests the expectation and leaves actual requirements with the responsible source and role.
check.feedbackIncorrect: One exchange does not establish a violation or the expectation’s full reach; an unsupported verdict can obscure the task. Confidence is not evidence of a formal responsibility, even when the colleague has useful expertise. Ignoring preparation altogether can abandon a legitimate requirement or helpful check. Clarify what the preview is meant to do and verify its actual status before choosing a change.

items.text: A colleague asked Rowan to obtain a preview before the meeting.
People may treat a preview as the sign that a draft is ready.
The senior analyst must formally approve every draft under an applicable instruction.
The draft instruction used the word ready without describing the preview.
New staff may learn the preview expectation only after a returned draft.
A designated review role has an actual sign-off responsibility for this task.

lessons.next: Next, examine how people learn different meanings of the same expectation.

scenario.context: DSD practice case: Rowan’s draft meets the listed preparation criteria, but a colleague asks for an unlisted private preview. The team is ready to record that the preview is DHS policy without checking.
scenario.prompt: What should the team record first?
options: The observed exchange, the possible expectation and the question for the actual instruction owner.
A definitive policy violation by the colleague.
A new mandatory approval rule based only on the colleague’s statement.
responses: This gives the team a careful starting point. The instruction owner can clarify the purpose and status before any change is proposed.
The available exchange does not establish a violation. A verdict cannot replace checking the actual rule and context.
A confident account does not delegate authority. Verify the responsibility rather than create it in a learning note.

lessons.transfer: Write a practice three-line map: what happened, what may be expected and which requirement needs verification. Use one task, not a personality description.

move.control: You can make an unclear expectation specific and examinable.
move.failure: An observation turns into an unsupported policy claim or motive verdict.
move.next: Choose one recurring work expectation and separate its evidence, meaning and verification question.

lessons.title: Understand how an expectation acquired meaning
lessons.summary: Examine learned ideas of competence and responsibility without profiling a colleague or a group.
lessons.objective: Identify the distinct learned meanings supplied by two colleagues.
objectives: Identify the distinct learned meanings supplied by two colleagues.
Explain how those meanings change an interpretation of asking for help.
Choose an adapted response that preserves the real task and does not require personal disclosure.
takeaways: The same work behavior can carry different learned meanings.
A person’s account can inform your understanding without describing a whole cultural group.
Adaptation changes the frame and response, not merely the label used for the other person.
lessons.statement: Ask what the action means before deciding what it says about the person.

image.caption: Colleagues clarify the purpose of a question before drawing a conclusion about competence.

intro.heading: Does asking first show care or dependence?
intro.body:
In a practice DSD research team, Dorian and Leena interpret an expectation to ask a senior colleague before presenting an unfamiliar finding. Dorian initially hears dependence. In earlier learning and work settings, Dorian was praised for forming an independent view before asking for help; a prepared explanation showed respect for another person’s time. Leena initially hears responsibility. In settings that shaped Leena, checking a consequential interpretation with someone who knows its history showed care for relationships and the people affected by the decision. Each voluntarily offers this account to explain the present work question.

These are specific learned meanings, not rules about a nationality, race, age or profession. Dorian and Leena may have other experiences that pull in different directions. They may also choose a different approach for another task. The accounts tell the team something about how these two people are interpreting this exchange. They do not authorize a profile of everyone with a similar identity or a claim that one person occupies a particular developmental stage.

At first, Dorian treats consultation as proof that the presenter has not done enough thinking. Leena treats independent presentation as a possible failure to consider shared history. Either conclusion can outrun the facts. Someone can ask a well-prepared question; someone can form an independent view while still checking an important dependency. Neither visible behavior establishes competence or care by itself. The actual finding, available evidence and applicable decision process still need examination.

The frame changes when Dorian recognizes that a question can protect the decision rather than surrender independent thought. Leena recognizes that preparation can honor another person’s contribution rather than reject it. The shared purpose becomes an adequately supported interpretation with relevant history considered. That purpose is broader than either person’s initial test of what a competent colleague should look like. It creates room for a more usable sequence.

An adapted response might ask the presenter to explain the provisional finding and the specific uncertainty, then identify whether a knowledgeable role should clarify historical context or an actual requirement. The presenter remains responsible for the work. The knowledgeable colleague contributes evidence within their role, rather than informally owning every judgment. If a designated sign-off is required, it retains its proper process. The change is not “everyone must ask more” or “everyone must be independent.” It connects the method to the actual question.

Keep inquiry respectful and voluntary. A colleague can explain which part of the task needs clarification without narrating a family history or naming a cultural affiliation. Dorian’s and Leena’s supplied histories are useful practice information, not a model for demanding private disclosure. You can ask, “What risk are you trying to avoid at this step?” or “What would a prepared question include?” These questions invite the meaning relevant to work while preserving personal choice.

Your own learning remains important even if the team changes no instruction. You can notice when you equate one familiar behavior with seriousness, competence or care. Consider where that expectation was learned, what it helps you do and where it may narrow your interpretation. The reflection can stay private. It is not a measure of someone else’s culture or a personnel assessment, and an insight does not excuse harmful conduct or erase a real obligation.

In this case, the useful adaptation is a shared method that honors preparation and consequential context. It begins with the provisional analysis, names the uncertainty, seeks the appropriate contribution and identifies the actual decision. That response follows meaning to a changed frame and then to a work choice. It helps the team coordinate without requiring either colleague to prove that their way is the only respectful one.

lessons.keyStatement: A changed interpretation should lead to a different, task-appropriate response rather than a new stereotype.

items.title: Recognize your starting test
items.body: Dorian first uses independence as the visible test of competence. Leena first uses checking with another person as the test of responsible care. Each test has a learned rationale, but neither establishes the quality of the current finding. Naming that starting point makes it possible to examine an assumption without treating the person who holds it as deficient.

items.title: Widen the interpretation
items.body: A prepared question can show independent thought and a wish to avoid an unsupported consequence. An independently developed finding can still invite relevant context. The shared frame is adequate reasoning with appropriate contribution. That change matters because it opens options the original either-or judgment could not see, while leaving the real evidence and authority intact.

items.title: Choose a fitting method
items.body: Ask for the provisional finding and its uncertainty. Seek the knowledgeable role’s specific contribution if relevant, and retain any actual sign-off. This does not require consultation for every ordinary choice or eliminate all collaboration. The method fits the consequence and task rather than making one learned style the permanent competence standard.

tabs.heading: Compare three interpretations of asking first

tabs.label: Dependence assumed
tabs.body: Dorian hears a question and assumes the presenter has not thought independently. That may discourage someone from identifying a genuine uncertainty and leave relevant history out of the decision. Ask what preparation has occurred and what the question concerns before drawing that conclusion. Independence can be valuable without becoming a requirement to conceal uncertainty. The revised response recognizes analysis and appropriate contribution as compatible, rather than testing competence through silence.

tabs.label: Responsibility assumed
tabs.body: Leena hears the absence of a prior check and assumes the presenter has ignored shared responsibility. The presenter may have considered relevant sources already or may be asking for context now. Clarify what needs checking and why. Collaboration can protect a decision without becoming an informal endorsement condition on every draft. The revised response keeps consequential context visible while allowing different legitimate ways to prepare and contribute.

tabs.label: Purpose clarified
tabs.body: The presenter explains a provisional interpretation and a specific question about earlier implementation. The team identifies a person who can clarify that history, distinguishes advice from any actual sign-off and returns the interpretation to its responsible owner. This method addresses both preparation and shared consequence. It does not promise agreement or assess either colleague’s cultural position. It changes the response because the meanings have widened the task frame.

check.question: What demonstrates adaptation in the Dorian and Leena case?
check.correct: Recognize their meanings the people describe, reframe preparation and consultation as compatible, and choose a method that fits the evidence question and actual responsibility.
wrong: Assign each person a fixed cultural profile from the behavior.
Require everyone to disclose a private background before raising a question.
Choose one colleague’s habit as the universal test of competence.
check.feedbackCorrect: The response moves from a learned interpretation to a wider frame and a concrete method. It preserves individual choice and the actual work responsibility.
check.feedbackIncorrect: A fixed profile converts two individual accounts into a group rule and prevents further inquiry. Required private disclosure is unnecessary to clarify a task and can narrow participation. Making one habit universal repeats the original either-or judgment rather than learning from the meanings. Identify the prepared reasoning, relevant uncertainty and appropriate contribution, then choose a response suited to this decision.

items.text: Dorian says prior settings praised independent preparation as respect for another person’s time.
The team sees that a prepared question can protect a consequential interpretation.
People who ask for help belong to a fixed low-competence cultural category.
Leena says earlier settings taught checking relevant history as care for shared consequences.
A presenter explains the finding and uncertainty before seeking the relevant role’s contribution.
Staff must disclose family histories to have their work question considered.

lessons.next: Next, map how an informal expectation is reinforced and whom its hidden steps burden.

scenario.context: DSD practice case: Dorian calls a prepared question dependent; Leena calls an independently prepared draft uncaring. Each has voluntarily explained a different learned meaning, and the team must examine the draft’s historical assumption.
options: Require the presenter to follow Leena’s habit for every future task.
Rank both colleagues on a cultural readiness scale.
Ask for the provisional reasoning and uncertainty, obtain the relevant historical contribution, and retain the actual decision role.
responses: Leena’s rationale is useful, but a universal habit still substitutes one meaning for task-specific reasoning.
The supplied accounts do not assess either person. A ranking would turn learning into an unsupported label.
This uses both meanings to widen the frame and choose a concrete response. Preparation and appropriate consultation can support the same well-grounded decision.

lessons.transfer: Using the practice accounts, write the initial interpretation, the new meaning it overlooked, the changed frame and the resulting work method. Keep your own reflection private if you prefer.

move.control: You can notice a learned assumption and widen the response it permits.
move.failure: A difference becomes a profile, a disclosure demand or a contest over one correct style.
move.next: At the next unfamiliar interaction, clarify the work meaning and purpose before making a competence or care judgment.

lessons.title: Map how the expectation is reinforced
lessons.summary: Examine who can see the cue, what follows it and whether it adds an avoidable burden.
lessons.objective: Map the cue, expected action and consequence in a practice draft-review pattern.
objectives: Map the cue, expected action and consequence in a practice draft-review pattern.
Distinguish a useful coordination purpose from an assumption that only insiders can interpret.
Identify one hidden burden and a work question that can examine it without inferring motive.
takeaways: An expectation is influential when the response to it shapes what people do next.
A familiar signal can be unclear to someone without the same history or role.
Making a cue understandable can preserve its useful purpose while removing guesswork.
lessons.statement: Examine the path from cue to consequence, not just whether the habit feels normal.

image.caption: A work map makes preparation, review and response visible to people joining the task.

intro.heading: A reaction is not an instruction
intro.body:
In a practice DSD review group, Priya joins a task midway through development. Long-serving colleagues use a quick reaction symbol in the shared discussion to mean they have seen the draft. Priya assumes the symbol means the recommendation is approved. Later, another colleague says the draft should never have moved forward without a written response from the review owner. The expectation was learned through earlier exchanges but not explained in the task instruction. The cue is visible; its meaning and consequence are not.

Map the pattern as a sequence. What cue does the person see? What action are they expected to take? What consequence follows if they interpret it differently? In this case, the symbol is the cue, waiting for a written owner response is the expected action, and a returned draft or delay is the possible consequence. A useful map also names who can confirm the meaning and what actual requirement applies. This prevents the exercise from becoming a list of people judged to know or miss the code.

Ask what the habit accomplishes. A quick acknowledgement may help colleagues know a message was received. That can be useful without carrying approval authority. The burden arises when the same signal is treated as enough guidance for experienced colleagues but leaves a newcomer guessing about the next step. The team can retain an acknowledgement and clarify that it is not the review decision. Removing every quick signal would be a much broader change than the evidence supports.

Look beyond individual misunderstanding. Does the task note identify the review owner? Does it distinguish acknowledgement, advice and approval? Is the required response available through a route people can actually use? If Priya must ask several colleagues privately to discover the next step, the hidden work includes finding the right person and reconciling conflicting answers. That effort may not appear in the project’s completion count. It is a process question worth examining, not proof that Priya lacks initiative.

An insider also can misread the signal when the task changes. Long experience does not make the cue reliable across new responsibilities. The team may have used it for an informal discussion and now be handling a recommendation that needs a particular review. State the current meaning and route rather than expecting history to fill the gap. The issue is not whether a person belongs to a category of insiders; it is whether the task path is understandable in its present context.

Consider an access question separately when it arises. If someone cannot use the material or makes an initial accommodation request, the actual request follows the appropriate route promptly; it does not wait for the team to finish mapping habits. Under Policy 1433, a request need not begin with special wording or a particular form, and a recipient who is not the appropriate contact should forward it promptly and notify the requester. General clearer instructions can be useful while the individual matter retains its proper process and information handling.

The map should also make room for unknown effects. A corrected note may make the cue easier to interpret, but the team cannot declare that everyone now understands it without relevant evidence. Ask whether the person could identify the next step in this task. Do not collect identity or health details to make the map feel complete, and do not turn a learning response into a competence ranking. The useful unit is the work path, not a profile of who learned it fastest.

For Priya’s case, a bounded improvement is to state the acknowledgement’s limited meaning, identify the actual review response and show where it appears. The expectation then becomes examinable: people no longer need to infer approval from a symbol. The team preserves the helpful cue while making its limit and the next action clear. That change targets the hidden burden without inventing a whole-team motive or a new decision authority.

inThisLesson: Separate general clarity and actual access requests.
lessons.keyStatement: A useful habit should not require people to guess its meaning or reconstruct the actual decision path.

items.title: Keep the cue and purpose distinct
items.body: A reaction can acknowledge receipt without approving a recommendation. Explain which meaning applies in this task, and identify the actual review response. The team can preserve efficient acknowledgement while avoiding a consequence built on a mistaken inference. Treating every cue as meaningless or every cue as approval both miss its limited purpose.

items.title: Make the discovery work visible
items.body: Priya asks several colleagues to identify the next step. That work is part of the practical path even if it does not appear as a formal task. Record what must be discovered and which instruction could clarify it. Do not assume the effort proves poor initiative or that every newcomer experiences the same problem; examine the particular burden and context.

items.title: Keep current access needs moving
items.body: A habit-mapping session is a general improvement exercise. It cannot become a prerequisite for an individual accommodation request or timely service help. Clarify the material where appropriate and use the actual responsible route for the current need. This allows a shared improvement and a protected individual process to proceed without putting private information into the map.

tabs.heading: Compare three responses to the unclear cue

tabs.label: Explain the task meaning
tabs.body: The team says the symbol means receipt, names the review owner and points to the actual written response. Priya can then distinguish being seen from being authorized to proceed. The instruction does not promise that the draft will pass or that every reaction elsewhere has the same meaning. It makes this path usable. The likely benefit is less reconstruction of the next step, which remains an intended effect to examine rather than a guaranteed result.

tabs.label: Blame the learner
tabs.body: The team calls Priya inattentive because experienced colleagues understood the cue. That comparison ignores the missing instruction and assumes everyone has the same history. It also leaves the next newcomer to repeat the discovery work. Examine whether the task actually explains the signal and decision path before making a personal conclusion. Experience can support a contribution without becoming proof that an unclear convention is adequate for everyone.

tabs.label: Remove every informal signal
tabs.body: The team bans acknowledgements rather than clarifying their scope. This may remove a useful way to see that a message arrived while leaving the approval route unclear. A larger change is not automatically more equitable or effective. Identify the exact confusion, retain a helpful function if appropriate and clarify the step that carries authority. The response should follow the observed mechanism rather than treat all informal coordination as suspect.

check.question: What should the team do when a reaction symbol means receipt to experienced colleagues but approval to Priya?
check.correct: Clarify the symbol’s limited meaning and the actual review route, while examining the discovery burden and preserving any current access response.
wrong: Call Priya inattentive because others know the convention.
Treat the symbol as formal approval to avoid explaining the route.
Ban every acknowledgement without checking what function it serves.
check.feedbackCorrect: This preserves useful coordination and makes the decision path explicit. It targets the hidden burden rather than label the person.
check.feedbackIncorrect: Calling Priya inattentive assumes shared history and leaves the unclear instruction unchanged. Treating acknowledgement as approval invents authority and can move work past an actual review. Banning every signal may remove a useful function without clarifying the required response. Identify the cue’s purpose, its limit and the next responsible step, then check whether that path is understandable.

items.text: A symbol shows that a colleague has seen the draft.
Priya asks several people to identify the actual next step.
Knowing the convention proves someone is more competent.
The draft needs the actual review owner’s written response before it proceeds.
An unclear signal leads to a returned draft and repeated preparation.
Any reaction automatically grants formal approval.

lessons.next: Next, verify where a habit ends and a real responsibility begins.

scenario.context: DSD practice case: Priya’s draft is returned after a reaction symbol was interpreted as approval. The task instruction does not explain the symbol or identify where the actual review response appears.
options: Label Priya a poor cultural fit and preserve the instruction unchanged.
State the acknowledgement’s scope, identify the actual review response and check whether the next step is usable.
Declare all informal communication prohibited by policy.
responses: That label does not explain the work path and is unsupported by the exchange. It leaves the same hidden task for another person.
This preserves useful acknowledgement and clarifies the consequential step. It does not infer universal understanding from the correction alone.
The case supports a specific clarification, not an invented blanket prohibition. Examine the function and actual requirement.

lessons.transfer: Map a practice cue, expected action, consequence and hidden discovery task. Add the instruction question that would make the next step understandable.

move.control: You can expose the extra work created by an unclear cue.
move.failure: The map ranks people or turns a signal into authority without evidence.
move.next: For one repeated handoff, make the cue’s purpose, limit and actual next step explicit through the responsible work process.

lessons.title: Verify the boundary between a habit and authority
lessons.summary: Keep expert advice, preparation and the actual decision distinct.
lessons.objective: Distinguish advice, preparation and authorized approval in a practice review map.
objectives: Distinguish advice, preparation and authorized approval in a practice review map.
Identify the source and responsible role needed to verify a claimed sign-off.
Choose a response that makes the route clear without bypassing a real obligation.
takeaways: Useful expertise does not automatically carry approval authority.
A formal responsibility should have a clear applicable source and route.
A map can expose a hidden decision without transferring that decision to the team.
lessons.statement: Make the decision visible without inventing who may make it.

image.caption: A team connects advice and preparation to the actual decision route.

intro.heading: Whose nod changes the status?
intro.body:
In a practice DSD procedure review, Erin prepares an updated instruction. Colleagues say that Quinn’s informal nod is required before it reaches the responsible review owner. Quinn has valuable experience but is not identified as the approval role in the current process. One colleague says the nod prevents rework; another says it makes the draft appear supported. Erin needs to distinguish useful advice from a hidden endorsement condition and the actual decision.

Start with the task’s consequence. The draft may clarify a work step, change a service expectation or involve an obligation another role must verify. Find the current applicable instruction and ask the responsible owner what is required. Do not decide authority from seniority, popularity or the number of colleagues who agree. A person can have excellent knowledge and still be providing advice rather than approval. A formal approver can also need expert input without handing the decision to that expert.

Map three contributions separately. Preparation develops the draft and its evidence. Advice identifies a question, correction or relevant history. Approval is the actual authorized decision within the process. The same person may perform more than one contribution when that is their real role, but the map should show the distinction. A label such as reviewed is not enough if people use it to mean three different things.

Ask what happens if Quinn is unavailable or disagrees. Can the drafter identify another appropriate source of context? Does the actual review owner still receive the draft and decide? Or is the work withheld until a personal endorsement is obtained? These questions reveal the mechanism without accusing Quinn of bad intent. The habit may have begun as useful quality support and acquired a different consequence. The team can examine that change while preserving the value of Quinn’s knowledge.

An explicit instruction can make the optional contribution easier to use. It might explain what kind of question benefits from an expert preview, how to request it and how the drafter records the unresolved issue for the actual owner. That gives staff a path when advice is needed without making a private relationship the only way forward. If an actual required review exists, document its real route rather than describe it as optional because the team prefers a shorter process.

DHS’s equity policy adds an important scope distinction for actual policy or practice work. The applicable equity-analysis requirement is not replaced by this course’s map. Use the actual DHS Toolkit or an appropriately consulted customized tool where the policy requires it, and preserve stated approvals for the long-term actions covered by that policy. The course can help expose the process question, but it is not a new approval instrument or permission to redesign a service rule.

A separate concern can also require a separate response. Suppose a manager hears that someone is being blocked from participation through protected-class harassment. That is not merely a habit to discuss at the next workshop. Policy 1436 requires managers and supervisors to report such complaints immediately to agency HR or the affirmative action officer. The general map can use a practice mechanism; the actual concern keeps its proper route and information handling. The team is not an investigation panel.

In Erin’s case, the bounded next step is to verify the review owner, clarify what Quinn’s advice contributes and remove any ambiguity about whether it is a prerequisite. The outcome may retain the preview, revise its timing or distinguish optional support from an actual required review. The useful result is a transparent route that connects knowledge to the real decision, rather than a team vote over whose nod should carry authority.

inThisLesson: Examine dependence on a private endorsement.
lessons.keyStatement: A transparent work route gives expertise a useful place and approval its actual place.

items.title: Describe the advice precisely
items.body: Quinn may clarify a history question or catch an unsupported assumption. Name that contribution instead of writing Quinn approved if no such role exists. The distinction helps Erin use the expertise and lets the actual owner see unresolved questions. It also avoids presenting a personal endorsement as the reason the draft can proceed.

items.title: Verify the approval route
items.body: Ask the current responsible owner to confirm the applicable review and sign-off. Use the real instruction and scope, not a learning group’s preference. If the route is unclear, show that as a question with an owner rather than quietly treating the most experienced person as the approver. A clear route is a practical coordination improvement.

items.title: Examine an unavailable colleague
items.body: If Quinn is absent, the task may need another appropriate source of knowledge or a visible unresolved question. Do not automatically skip a required review or stop all work until a colleague whose input is optional returns. The correct response depends on the contribution needed. Showing that dependency helps the team plan without reducing quality or making progress depend on one private relationship.

tabs.heading: Compare review labels and their effects

tabs.label: Prepared
tabs.body: Erin has developed the draft and checked the identified evidence. This supports a preparation claim. It does not mean a required policy review has occurred or that every relevant concern is resolved. A useful preparation record names the sources examined and the question still open. The actual review owner can then assess the work without guessing whether a confident ready label contains a hidden endorsement or a formal decision.

tabs.label: Advised
tabs.body: Quinn has offered a specific correction or interpretation. The drafter should consider the contribution and explain how it informed the draft, while keeping the unresolved question visible if necessary. Advice can improve the work without automatically authorizing its release. If disagreement remains, bring the reason and evidence to the actual responsible role rather than count supporters. This gives knowledge influence without confusing influence with the decision.

tabs.label: Approved
tabs.body: The authorized role has made the applicable decision within its real scope. Identify that decision accurately instead of relying on a vague reviewed label. Approval for one step may not cover another responsibility, and a preparer’s task map cannot expand it. The practical benefit is that colleagues can see what may proceed and what still needs action. It makes the next step clearer without adding an invented committee or a universal consultant gate.

check.question: Quinn offers useful advice but is not identified as the approval role. What should Erin’s map show?
check.correct: The specific advice, the applicable review requirement and the actual decision role, with any unresolved authority question kept visible.
wrong: Quinn’s seniority automatically makes the informal nod formal approval.
A team vote can waive any applicable policy review.
Optional advice must be removed because only approvers can contribute knowledge.
check.feedbackCorrect: This gives useful expertise a place while keeping actual approval and required process distinct.
check.feedbackIncorrect: Seniority and expertise do not automatically delegate sign-off authority. A team vote cannot waive an applicable requirement or grant a power the team lacks. Removing all advice also misses the value of relevant knowledge in preparing a sound decision. Clarify the contribution and actual role, then use the appropriate process for any unresolved requirement.

items.text: Quinn identifies a historical assumption the drafter should examine.
The current instruction names a responsible approval role.
A popular colleague’s nod authorizes every service change.
Erin records the evidence checked and the unresolved question.
A required policy review has a stated scope and appropriate route.
A learning group votes to waive every formal review.

lessons.next: Next, turn the verified map into a workable agreement.

scenario.context: DSD practice case: Erin’s draft is held for Quinn’s private nod. Quinn provides expert advice, while a different role owns the actual review. The task instruction does not explain whether the preview is optional.
scenario.prompt: Which response makes the path clearer?
options: Declare Quinn the approver because colleagues trust the advice.
Send the draft without any actual required review.
Verify the real route, explain the purpose of the preview and distinguish advice from the authorized decision.
responses: Trust can make advice valuable but does not establish approval authority. Keep the contribution and decision distinct.
The hidden condition does not authorize bypassing a real requirement. Clarify the route rather than remove safeguards wholesale.
This connects preparation, expertise and the actual decision. It makes the expectation usable without inventing powers or a verdict about motives.

lessons.transfer: Draw a practice preparation-to-decision path. Label advice and approval separately, and identify the source or role that can confirm any claimed prerequisite.

move.control: You can make an authority question visible instead of silently solving it through seniority.
move.failure: Expertise becomes a hidden approval condition or a team map bypasses a real review.
move.next: Verify one consequential review label and clarify what it permits in the actual work route.

lessons.title: Develop a clear work agreement
lessons.summary: Preserve the useful purpose, explain a concrete method and make its limits understandable.
lessons.objective: Draft an explicit work agreement that addresses a practice hidden preparation burden.
objectives: Draft an explicit work agreement that addresses a practice hidden preparation burden.
Compare the agreement’s purpose, method, responsibility and exception route.
Identify a promised change that exceeds the team’s actual authority or leaves a new burden hidden.
takeaways: A useful agreement explains what to do, why it matters and where a question goes.
Keep the good purpose rather than replace one invisible rule with another.
The agreement must fit the actual work and decision responsibility.
lessons.statement: Replace guesswork with an understandable path that people can use.

image.caption: Colleagues develop a shared instruction with an explicit purpose and next step.

intro.heading: From always ask first to a usable preparation path
intro.body:
In a practice DSD working group, Stefan proposes replacing the expectation to always ask a senior colleague first. New staff say it is unclear what to ask, whom to approach or when the answer is enough. Experienced staff explain that the preview was intended to catch consequential assumptions before a recommendation is used. The group has verified that the current instruction requires a responsible review but not one particular colleague’s endorsement. It can now develop a better preparation method within that scope.

Keep the useful purpose visible: supported recommendations with consequential uncertainty identified. The method might ask preparers to state the proposed interpretation, the evidence considered and the question that still needs a knowledgeable contribution. A contact route can identify which role handles the question and how to proceed if the usual person to ask is unavailable. The actual required review remains where it belongs. This is more usable than replacing always ask first with never ask.

An explicit agreement needs enough detail to guide a task without trying to anticipate every circumstance. Name the action, its purpose, responsibility and next route. In this case, a short preparation note can distinguish a known fact, a provisional interpretation and a question for the person responsible. The person responsible can explain what is resolved and what still needs another role. The note should fit the real task and use appropriately protected information. Its value is clarity, not a longer form for its own sake.

Compare the burden of the new method with the old one. A clear question route may reduce private reconstruction, but an added note can create work if it duplicates an existing record. Look at the whole path. Can the same information be used in the actual review rather than copied into a separate learning document? Who answers the question, and do they have the capacity and responsibility? A proposal that simply moves discovery work to another colleague has not made the burden disappear.

Invite relevant perspectives on whether the path can be used. A person new to the task can examine whether the instruction explains the next step. An experienced preparer can identify a consequential context it misses. The actual review owner can confirm the responsibility. These contributions are different and useful; no participant automatically represents everyone with a similar identity or role. If the proposal affects a service process, appropriate service knowledge and affected perspectives belong in the actual work, beyond this team exercise.

Explain what is decided and what remains open. Staff can help develop a method without acquiring authority over every related service rule or resource. The consultant can support the inquiry with guidance and feedback while the team prepares the work. A clear pending question is preferable to a promise that the consultant or workshop can approve anything. Once the responsible role confirms the agreed scope, staff should know how the method fits the real process.

Use an exception route rather than a rule of silence. If the note does not fit an urgent task or the knowledgeable role is unavailable, identify the actual work-planning or escalation contact. Do not require people to conceal uncertainty to appear independent, or wait indefinitely for an informal endorsement. A practical agreement should help surface the unresolved issue so an authorized person can respond. Its exceptions cannot erase current required duties.

Finally, make a review question part of the agreement. Ask whether preparers can identify the review owner and convey the consequential uncertainty without repeated private searches. That question connects the method to its intended effect. It leaves room to revise the instruction if it duplicates work or fails to clarify the route. The agreement is a way to make coordination more understandable, not a declaration that the team has solved culture or that every person should use an identical style.

lessons.keyStatement: A clear agreement connects purpose, action and response without creating a new hidden prerequisite.

accordion.heading: Build the agreement around the task

items.title: State an action someone can carry out
items.body: Instead of ask appropriately, say what a preparer should make clear: the proposed interpretation, evidence considered and consequential question. The person responsible can respond to those elements. The action is concrete enough to use and does not demand a private history or a preferred personality style. Check whether an existing record already contains the information before adding a duplicate note.

items.title: Name a responsive route
items.body: The preparer needs to know which role handles the unresolved issue, what is expected from the review and where a question goes if the usual contact is unavailable. A list of names alone may not explain the responsibility. Show the role and task connection so the instruction can remain understandable when people change, without promising an invented deadline or approval power.

items.title: Check the whole-path burden
items.body: A new method may save discovery time while adding recording or response work. Examine both. If all questions are moved to one unplanned helper, the team has shifted the burden rather than arranged the needed support. Use the actual responsible roles to consider capacity and revise the method. The best agreement is not necessarily the shortest or most elaborate one; it is the one that supports the task within real constraints.

tabs.label: Keep the vague rule
tabs.body: “Always ask a senior person first” leaves the preparer to choose a person, explain an uncertain question and infer whether the response permits proceeding. It may preserve useful quality support for those who know the history, but keeps discovery work hidden. Clarify the type of contribution and actual review. A shared instruction should explain what people need to do rather than make familiarity with private relationships the route to success.

tabs.label: Replace it with a rigid opposite
tabs.body: “Never ask until the analysis is complete” may sound empowering but can discourage appropriate uncertainty and delay a needed historical or technical contribution. Independence and consultation are not opposites. Ask for a prepared interpretation and a specific question at the point they can help the work. The method should fit the consequence, not require every task to demonstrate one ideal style.

tabs.label: Make the path explicit
tabs.body: “State the interpretation and evidence, identify a consequential uncertainty and use the named role’s route before the required review” gives the preparer something concrete to do. The responsible role still needs to confirm the method and capacity. The agreement can then be tested through a scoped task rather than assumed effective from its clear wording. It preserves the quality purpose while making the question and next step available without guesswork.

check.question: Which proposal best replaces the vague ask-first expectation?
check.correct: An authorized preparation path that states the purpose, what the preparer explains, the relevant contribution route and a question for reviewing the method.
wrong: Keep the rule vague so newcomers learn initiative by guessing.
Require independent completion of every task without relevant questions.
Promise the new learning note replaces all actual policy reviews.
check.feedbackCorrect: The proposal preserves the purpose and makes the method and response explicit, with its effectiveness still open to examination.
check.feedbackIncorrect: Guessing leaves the discovery burden hidden and does not explain what initiative should accomplish. A blanket ban on questions can omit relevant evidence and turn one style into the standard. A learning note cannot replace actual required policy review or approval. Make the preparation and contribution path concrete, use the responsible scope and check whether the method helps rather than only looks tidy.

items.text: The instruction explains which consequential uncertainty the preparer should identify.
The proposed question route needs a confirmed responsible role and capacity.
Every new question is sent to one unplanned helper without arranging the work.
The agreement distinguishes advice from the actual required review.
The method’s effect will be checked using a scoped task rather than assumed.
The learning note claims to waive all applicable policy approvals.

lessons.next: Next, examine whether the new method actually changes the path.

scenario.context: DSD practice case: Stefan’s group proposes a clearer preparation note. It identifies a consequential uncertainty, but sends all questions to one colleague who has no assigned response role. The group calls the change complete.
options: Keep the note’s useful purpose and resolve the actual response responsibility, capacity and whole-path burden before claiming the route works.
Declare the single helper responsible for every answer without involving the work owner.
Return to an unexplained rule because explicit instructions always reduce initiative.
responses: The proposal is promising but not yet a functioning route. A responsible response and review question make its use examinable.
A learning group cannot silently assign another person’s work or authority. Arrange the real responsibility and capacity.
The case shows a dependency, not a reason to restore guesswork. Revise the method around the actual task.

lessons.transfer: Draft a practice agreement with purpose, preparer action, response role, exception route and review question. Identify one dependency rather than hide it in the word agreed.

move.control: You can turn an informal expectation into a specific, reviewable proposal.
move.failure: A clearer form hides an unarranged response or creates another condition only insiders understand.
move.next: Develop one task agreement with the responsible roles and examine its whole-path burden before treating it as in use.

lessons.title: Review the practice and your own assumptions
lessons.summary: Separate an instruction change, an observed result and what remains unknown.
lessons.objective: Distinguish delivery, scoped task evidence and unsupported cultural or causal conclusions.
objectives: Distinguish delivery, scoped task evidence and unsupported cultural or causal conclusions.
Identify whether a practice new method removed or shifted a discovery burden.
Choose a concrete revision and a private reflection question grounded in the reviewed task.
takeaways: A new instruction shows a change was made, not that the expectation has changed everywhere.
Review the task and response, including any burden moved to another role.
Personal growth and work evidence are useful without turning either into a score about colleagues.
lessons.statement: Review the actual path, then choose the next useful improvement.

image.caption: A team examines a specific work change and the question that remains.

intro.heading: Does the clearer agreement work?
intro.body:
In a practice DSD trial, Mina’s team uses a revised preparation path for four handoffs. The instruction now distinguishes acknowledgement, advice and the actual review response. Two drafts are returned for missing evidence; two proceed after review. A project note says unwritten rules have been eliminated and the whole team is now culturally competent. Those conclusions do not follow from the limited task evidence. The instruction changed and four handoffs occurred; the broader experience and cause remain open.

Begin with the purpose the agreement was intended to serve. Could a preparer identify the review owner and explain the consequential uncertainty without reconstructing the path privately? A returned draft is not automatically a failure of the agreement if the review identifies genuinely missing evidence. A draft that proceeds is not automatically proof that the instructions were usable. Examine the actual reason, route and context rather than use pass or return as a culture score.

Check whether the hidden work changed. One preparer may still need three private conversations to find the correct contact. Another may use the stated route but wait because response capacity was never arranged. The instruction may be clearer while the practical dependency remains unresolved. This is a useful finding. It suggests a specific revision or arrangement rather than a total verdict that the method succeeded or failed.

Use comparable evidence when comparing periods. Earlier counts may include a different kind of draft or record only formal returns, while the trial captures informal questions too. An apparent increase in questions may reflect a more visible route rather than a worse process. Describe that definition difference and what it allows you to conclude. The practice four handoffs are a small scoped practice account, not a representative measure or proof of cause.

Ask for feedback about the task with an appropriate purpose and handling. Could the preparer locate the next step? Did the person responsible receive the needed question? Was information duplicated? A colleague’s account can identify a problem and help revise the path without representing everyone. Missing responses remain unknown, and a recognizable small-group story is not automatically anonymous because names were removed. Use practice material in the learning activity and actual information only through the proper work process.

Notice reinforcement as well as wording. If the instruction welcomes a prepared question but the response mocks anyone who asks, the practical expectation still rewards silence. If a clear route exists but praise goes only to those who obtain a private endorsement, the old condition may continue alongside the new note. Describe that specific mismatch and consider the appropriate response. A document cannot change every interaction by itself; the way people answer and recognize work also matters.

Private reflection can develop alongside the task review. Ask whether you still interpret a question as dependence, a lack of endorsement as disrespect or a returned draft as evidence about the person’s worth. Revisit the alternative meaning and the response it might support. You can keep this reflection personal, and nobody needs an inferred IDI position or cultural ranking to do it. The aim is a wider understanding and a deliberate next interaction, not a public declaration of progress.

For Mina’s team, the next note can report the instruction delivered, the four handoffs’ actual scope, a remaining response dependency and one revision for the responsible role. It should distinguish the useful result from the unanswered question. The team can retain a sound element, adjust a specific part and continue examining the method. That is meaningful follow-through on an unwritten expectation without promising that all hidden rules, cultural differences or access barriers have been resolved.

inThisLesson: Examine response as well as wording.
Choose a revision and private reflection.
lessons.keyStatement: A precise review can support a useful next action without claiming complete cultural change.

accordion.heading: Review what the evidence can show

items.title: Check the actual task question
items.body: The method was intended to make the review route usable. Ask whether preparers could find it and convey a consequential uncertainty, not only whether drafts passed. A return for missing evidence may show the review did its job. A return caused by an unclear prerequisite points to a different issue. The reason and path make the count meaningful.

items.title: Notice the new receiving work
items.body: A question route can make uncertainty visible and add response work to another role. Examine that work and the actual arrangement rather than assume the burden disappeared from the preparer’s experience. A clearer instruction may remain useful while capacity needs attention. The review should connect those two findings, allowing a specific next decision instead of a blanket success claim.

items.title: Revisit your learned interpretation
items.body: You may notice that you still hear a prepared question as weakness or treat an endorsement as the only sign of care. Return to the individual meanings examined earlier and ask which part of the actual task matters now. Choose a different response you can practice. This reflection need not be public and does not determine anyone’s assessed position or personnel status.

tabs.label: Instruction delivered
tabs.body: The revised note explains the preparation and review route. This is an action completed and can be verified in the material. It does not establish that everyone used it or that informal reactions now match it. Keep that delivery claim because it matters, then examine the task and response. A useful review need not choose between celebrating the action and acknowledging that its result is still only partly known.

tabs.label: Scoped path examined
tabs.body: Four handoffs provide evidence about particular tasks under the trial conditions. Describe whether the next step was located, why drafts were returned and what response work remained. The limited account can support a correction to the instruction or an arrangement for questions. It cannot establish a permanent outcome for the whole team. State its scope so the next decision can use the evidence without treating a small number as universal proof.

tabs.label: Broad culture declared
tabs.body: “All unwritten rules are gone” or “everyone is culturally competent” goes beyond the instruction and handoff evidence. It can also hide a useful unresolved issue by making the review feel finished. Replace the broad label with the actual task finding, unknowns and next action. Personal learning can be meaningful without a score, while the team’s practice still needs specific evidence and follow-through.

check.question: What can Mina’s team accurately conclude from the revised note and four handoffs?
check.correct: The instruction was delivered; report the handoffs’ scoped task evidence, remaining burden and next revision without claiming complete cultural change or cause.
wrong: Two drafts proceeding prove every hidden expectation is gone.
Two returned drafts prove the whole team is resistant to change.
The pilot allows an individual cultural competence ranking for every staff member.
check.feedbackCorrect: This retains the useful action and task findings while keeping their scope and unknowns honest.
check.feedbackIncorrect: Two successful review paths cannot establish that every expectation disappeared or every person had the same experience. Two returned drafts also cannot establish resistance; they may lack evidence or reveal a specific route problem. A task pilot does not assess individual cultural competence or justify a personnel ranking. Examine the reasons, response path and receiving work, then choose the proportionate next action.

items.text: The revised instruction distinguishes acknowledgement from the actual review response.
The trial does not establish how every person experienced the path.
Four handoffs prove the whole team is culturally competent.
Two drafts were returned for missing evidence within the stated trial.
The response role’s capacity needs examination before the route is called dependable.
A returned draft identifies the employee’s fixed cultural stage.

lessons.next: Use the job aid to map one expectation, develop a clear agreement and review its actual effect.

scenario.context: DSD practice case: Mina’s team has a clearer note and four trial handoffs. One preparer still needed several private contacts, while the report claims all hidden rules are eliminated.
scenario.prompt: Which revision makes the report useful?
options: Keep the universal claim because the note is clear.
Report the specific change and trial context, examine the remaining discovery burden and name the next responsible revision.
Publish a cultural ranking based on who asked the fewest questions.
responses: Clear wording is useful but does not establish that the actual path is dependable for everyone. The remaining burden deserves examination.
This connects evidence to a concrete improvement without losing the value of the work already done. It leaves broader conclusions unclaimed.
The number of questions does not establish a cultural position or competence. It may reflect the task, route and context.

lessons.transfer: Write a practice review note: intended task effect, instruction delivered, scoped evidence, remaining burden and next revision. Add a private question about an interpretation you want to reconsider.

move.control: You can keep the review precise and turn an unresolved issue into a useful next action.
move.failure: A clear document becomes a universal culture verdict or a task count becomes a person score.
move.next: Review one use of the agreed path, identify what helped and revise one unresolved mechanism through the responsible role.

jobAid.subtitle: A practical map for one unwritten expectation and a clearer work agreement.
remember: Describe the exchange before deciding what it means.
Distinguish observation, informal expectation and verified requirement.
Use a person’s supplied meaning without turning it into a group profile.
Preserve the helpful purpose while making action and response clear.
Review the actual task and burden; do not score people or declare all culture changed.

sections.heading: Map the expectation
items: What cue appears, what action is expected and what consequence follows?
How is a person expected to learn the step?
What useful purpose might the habit serve?
Which part is observed, inferred or an actual requirement to verify?

sections.heading: Examine meaning and responsibility
items: What meaning am I bringing to the exchange?
What individual meaning has the person freely supplied, and how does it change my interpretation?
Which contribution is preparation, advice or actual approval?
What source and role can confirm a claimed prerequisite?
Does a current access request or formal concern need its own timely response?

sections.heading: Develop and review the agreement
items: Explain purpose, preparer action, response role and a practical exception route.
Check added, duplicated and receiving work before treating the proposal as in use.
State what is decided and what remains a dependency.
Examine the scoped task result, response pattern and missing evidence.
Choose one revision and one private reflection question.

sources.title: Council of Europe — Developing intercultural competence through education
sources.note: Explores varied affiliations, learned meanings and inquiry into perspectives. The Dorian and Leena examples, habit map and agreement exercises are learning activities, not group profiles, assessments or Minnesota policy requirements.

sources.title: Minnesota Management and Budget — Respectful Workplace Policy 1432
sources.note: Actual respectful conduct and concern process. A learning map supports examination of work and does not decide a violation, require private confrontation or replace a proper concern route.

sources.title: Minnesota Management and Budget — Harassment and Discrimination Prohibited Policy 1436
sources.note: Actual manager and supervisor immediate reporting to HR or the affirmative action officer for covered complaints. A protected-class concern cannot wait for a general habit-mapping exercise.

sources.title: Minnesota Management and Budget — ADA Reasonable Accommodation Policy 1433
sources.note: Actual initial request and responsible forwarding process. A shared instruction change does not replace an individual request, authorize medical collection or delay the appropriate response.

sources.title: Minnesota Department of Human Services — Equity Policy
sources.note: The actual equity-analysis requirement and stated approval scope remain distinct from this optional learning map. Applicable Toolkit or appropriately consulted customized-tool work is not replaced by a team agreement.
